chunks: As for what Muhammad b. Ahmad b. Yahya reported from Muhammad b. 'Isa from al-Hasan b. Rashid —
He said: I asked him about garments made in Basra in the style of Yemeni qasab, from raw silk and cotton: is it proper that the dead be shrouded in them?
He said: If the cotton is more than the raw silk, there is no objection.

[al-Tusi:] This does not contradict what we have previously stated, for we only forbid garments in which salat is not permissible — even though pure cotton is preferable. This narration is interpreted as indicating permissibility, not preference. And what further indicates that linen is makruh is in addition to what has already been stated.

key_terms.الْجَوَازِ: permissibility (jawaz) — the lower jurisprudential grade distinguishing what is allowed from what is recommended or preferred
key_terms.قَزٍّ: raw/wild silk — a fabric whose predominance in a kafan renders it impermissible
key_terms.قُطْنٍ: cotton — the preferred material for the burial shroud; must predominate over silk for the shroud to be valid
key_terms.مَكْرُوهٌ: makruh — jurisprudentially reprehensible but not haram; here applied to linen as a shroud material

ai.seo_question: Can burial shrouds (kafan) made from a mixture of raw silk and cotton be used according to Shia jurisprudence, and what is the ruling on linen shrouds?
ai.summary: Al-Hasan b. Rashid asked the Imam whether Basran garments woven in the Yemeni qasab style — a blend of raw silk (qazz) and cotton — may be used as burial shrouds (kafan). The Imam permits their use on condition that the cotton content exceeds the silk. Sheikh al-Tusi then provides a jurisprudential gloss: this ruling does not contradict the principle that only garments permissible for salat may serve as a kafan; pure cotton remains the preferred option and this report establishes permissibility (jawaz) rather than virtue (fadl), with the additional note that linen carries a degree of reprehensibility (karahah).
